endorsements.quote: In health care and research, this means using data sets that reflect the diversity of the target population and actively involving subject matter experts from different backgrounds in iterative model design.

For example, if a hospital uses AI to help draft patient messages and responses, input should be solicited from community or patient advisory boards that reflect the demographics of the population served.

Partnering with trusted community leaders, advocacy organizations, and patients in the design and evaluation of AI-generated patient-facing applications can help identify potential biases, misinterpretations, or unintended harms before implementation.
Feedback loops should be ongoing, not one-time events, to foster transparency, accountability, and trust.
Training should emphasize that AI is not neutral; its outputs reflect the biases embedded in its training data.
All neurologists should be prepared to critically engage with AI.

Policy frameworks should also establish clear accountability mechanisms for failures of AI tools to perform as intended, including pathways for patients and health care professionals to report concerns about bias or inaccurate outputs.

AI governance should not be a one-time regulatory process, but an ongoing, adaptive effort that evolves alongside technological advancements.

As AI tools are increasingly integrated into clinical research and care delivery, institutional review boards must be equipped to assess issues related to algorithmic bias, data privacy, and participant protections.

Health and research institutions must regularly evaluate data governance policies that clearly define how patient data, including digital phenotyping and behavioral metadata, are collected, stored, and shared.

unlisted_practices: Establish an independent, patient-centered authority to oversee health-related AI and ensure alignment with core bioethical principles.
Strengthen institutional review board capacity to evaluate AI-related research protocols.
Ensure HIPAA compliance in AI use.
Provide transparent consent processes, limits on secondary data use, and mechanisms for patients to access or delete their data.
Professional societies should integrate AI-related policy issues into their advocacy efforts.
Train neurologists to assess the inclusivity and trustworthiness of AI tools their patients encounter.
Continuously evolve AI education and training to reflect current trends and new challenges.
